scenes.text: Syllabus four point four solve simple problems which may be modelled as the motion of connected particles. By the end, you can use the string conditions. Write an equation for each particle. And follow the motion when the string goes slack.

scenes.title: Watch the whole motion first

beats.text: Consider two particles hanging from a string over a pulley. The heavier particle, P, starts lower than Q.
Release them. P speeds up downwards, pulling Q upwards. The pulley turns as the string passes over it.
P lands. The string slackens.
Gravity slows Q, and it stops. How high did Q get?

scenes.title: The complete question

beats.text: Here is the full problem. P has mass three kilograms.
Q has mass one kilogram.
Initially, P is zero point eight metres above the floor.
Q is one metre above the floor.
Both are released from rest. Take g as ten metres per second squared.
The string is light and inextensible, initially taut, over a fixed smooth light pulley. Ignore air resistance.
P stays on the floor without rebounding. Q has clearance below the pulley. The string goes slack after P lands.
Find the maximum height of Q above the floor. We will find acceleration, tension, and the speed at impact along the way. Read the givens before we start.

scenes.title: What the string conditions tell us

beats.text: While the inextensible string is taut, each length gained on one side is lost on the other. P falls as far as Q rises.
Their speeds and acceleration magnitudes are equal. Their acceleration vectors point in opposite directions.
Because the string is light and the pulley smooth, the tension has the same magnitude on both sides. It pulls each particle upwards.
Equal tensions do not mean balanced forces on either particle. Isolate each body. Choose down positive for P and up positive for Q.
Which particle has weight greater than tension?
P does: its resultant and acceleration are downwards. For Q, tension exceeds weight, giving an upward resultant.

scenes.title: Stage 1: acceleration and tension

beats.text: Start with Newton's second law: resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
For P, down is positive. Weight minus tension equals its mass times acceleration.
Substitute three for the mass and ten for g. Thirty minus T equals three a.
For Q, up is positive. Tension minus weight equals mass times acceleration.
Its mass is one, and g is ten. So T minus ten equals a.
Add these scalar equations, with their own positive directions. The tensions cancel algebraically. Twenty equals four a.
Divide both sides by four. The common acceleration magnitude is five metres per second squared. P down, Q up.
Now use Q's equation to find tension. T equals its mass multiplied by the sum of g and a.
One times ten plus five gives a tension of fifteen newtons.

scenes.title: Stage 1: speed as P hits the floor

beats.text: P falls zero point eight metres to the floor. While the string is taut, Q rises the same zero point eight metres.
What speed has Q gained? Use its upward motion, starting from rest.
The constant acceleration formula is v squared equals u squared plus two a s.
The initial speed is zero, acceleration five, and upward displacement zero point eight.
Therefore v squared is eight square metres per square second. Keep this squared speed: it passes directly into the next stage.
Taking the positive square root, the speed is square root eight metres per second. Keeping v squared as eight avoids rounding in stage two.
Q's height at impact is its initial height plus this rise.
One plus zero point eight is one point eight metres above the floor. This is not yet the maximum.

scenes.title: Stage 2: the string is slack

beats.text: Now P is on the floor. Q continues upwards, leaving slack string. The tension is zero: a string cannot push.
For Q, up remains positive. Weight is now its only force, so acceleration is minus g. The old common acceleration no longer applies.
Its initial squared speed for this stage is eight. At maximum height its speed is zero. Let the extra rise be d.
Again, v squared equals u squared plus two a s.
Substitute zero for the final speed, eight for the initial squared speed, and minus ten for acceleration.
Move twenty d to the left. Twenty d equals eight.
Divide by twenty. The extra rise is zero point four metres.
Maximum height equals initial height, plus the rise while taut, plus the extra rise.
One plus zero point eight plus zero point four gives two point two metres above the floor.

scenes.title: Use the conditions at each stage

beats.text: What changes with a smooth table? A horizontal block and a hanging block still have equal acceleration magnitudes while connected. The directions are now right and down.
For the table block, vertical weight and reaction balance. Tension is its horizontal resultant. Apply Newton's law separately to each body.
Use the string conditions. Light string and smooth pulley give equal tension; taut and inextensible gives the linked motion.
